reader.summary: Australia's week was defined by a mix of sporting disappointment, an international justice milestone, and domestic economic recalibration. In rugby, Australia beat Scotland with an eight-try display but then lost badly to New Zealand 43-21 in the second Bledisloe test in Sydney, with the All Blacks dominating the first half. In rugby league, the Wallabies edged New Zealand 24-22 in the World Cup opener. Three men in Mexico were each sentenced to 158 years in prison for the murders of an Australian and a US surfer, closing out a case that had gripped both countries. Greenpeace activists occupied a Woodside natural-gas project unit off Western Australia, briefly pausing operations and intensifying the energy-transition debate. A hidden video camera was discovered in the women's shower of an Australian navy ship, prompting a formal inquiry. The first confirmed H5N1 bird-flu case was reported on sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island, raising biosecurity concerns. On the economic front, September employment data showed a rise in unemployment, easing pressure for further rate hikes and damping home-auction activity. Australia also received its first Michelin stars, with eleven restaurants in a single state recognised, and Victoria approved the country's largest wind-power project. The 3M 'forever chemicals' lawsuit entered a new legal phase as the company argued the A$1.4 billion claim was structurally flawed.

3M told an Australian court it would argue the A$1.4 billion 'forever chemicals' class-action lawsuit was legally flawed.

The Wallabies edged New Zealand 24-22 in the Rugby League World Cup opener with Bostock scoring three tries.

display.eli5:
Next week is all about sport and a gas-platform fight in Australia. The biggest story on the field is the second Test cricket match against South Africa. Australia won the first Test, and South Africa is coming back with a reshuffled lineup to try and steal a win. Expect a tense, close match, and low crowds are already making officials rethink the whole format.

The other big sporting event is the Rugby League World Cup, where Australia barely beat New Zealand 24-22 in the opening game. The next group-stage match will test whether the league side can handle a full tournament schedule.

Off the field, Greenpeace activists are still tied to a Woodside gas platform off Western Australia. Woodside will have to make a big call about whether to restart the rig or sue the protesters, and that decision will ripple through the country's energy debate.

A surprise to watch for: banks in Australia are pulling back from financing private credit funds. If one of the big banks suddenly tightens its lending rules, it could send ASX property and infrastructure stocks into a short but sharp drop.
